items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: Marshall Stearns was running a column in Downbeat. And sort of a history of jazz as he called it.

ctx.x: Was there any written guides at that time that you would have had to go by?

The first book that came out that I ever saw was Schleman or Schleman, how do you pronounce it? Schleman, that sounds like a famous name. It's an English show. It came out about 1936 and then Delaunay came out about the next year or so I'd say. Around 37. These were discographies. So yeah the discography, the first edition of that. So and then George, not George Haver, at first Marshall Stearns was running a column in Downbeat. And sort of a history of jazz as he called it. So he would sometimes talk about…
He was in New York I think.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: he said, if you all don't dig up some real documentary dope, we'll call it, on Bolden by the New York people, like Meaden, Marshall Stearns, and all the other New York authors, are just going to cross him off the list as really never having existed.

ctx.x: I have a record he made with Joe Dierensburg. He might have played a little bit after that, not much.

So, because he, I heard. The LARP record? Yeah. It was made about that time, actually. He had cancer, I heard, at that time. He looked in pretty good health and talked like he'd be playing, like he was alright. But a couple years later, maybe about two years ago, he died. So, evidently he did have cancer. And he was one of the better drummers, not flashy in any way either. And maybe in some sense, monotonous compared to some of the other New Orleans drummers, but still a wonderful rhythm section. Buster Wilson…
